name: Anishinaabe
packetScope: Four substantive community-published works: one renewed Citizen Potawatomi Nation museum account and three new Pokagon, Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa, and Forest County Potawatomi perspectives. Specific nations remain distinct within broader relationships. No canonical/Site edits.

sources.title: Prophetic wisdom: The first of 11 new exhibits, the Seven Fires sets tribe on path to its future
sources.author: Citizen Potawatomi Nation; no individual byline displayed
sources.annotation: A dated account of the Cultural Heritage Center's public exhibit, with named staff and artist perspectives. Read as Citizen Potawatomi interpretation. Prophetic details, sacred symbolism and precise migration chronology are not reproduced or made universal; its Three Fires role labels differ from other community accounts.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual complete article body, paragraphs on the reopening, Kelli Mosteller's and Jennifer Randell's interpretation, and concluding continuity statements; web lines41–67.

sources.title: Our Culture / Neshnabé bmadzëwen — History
sources.author: Pokagon Band of Potawatomi; institutional account, no individual byline displayed
sources.annotation: Substantive public history from a particular Potawatomi government. Useful for differences within related peoples and continuity through removal pressures. Legal summaries, casualty estimates and court details are not independently established here. Other ritual and clan sections are outside the selected synthesis.
sources.publicationDate: Undated; footer year is not treated as publication date
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual History section, web lines511–522, and introductory culture paragraphs499–503. Linked videos, archives and other sections not claimed as reviewed works.

sources.title: Our Land and Culture: A 200 Year History of Our Land Use
sources.author: Wesley L. Andrews, research and writing; Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians community project
sources.publisher: Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians
sources.type: Community-published historical book with elder interviews
sources.annotation: A tribal project combining documents and elder interviews, with youth participation. Its own introduction limits later history to Waganakising bands, including Beaver Islands, and distinguishes shared identity from specific belonging. Selected pages only; neither a full-book review nor current legal interpretation. Historical vocabulary and family records are not replicated.
sources.publicationDate: November 2005; cover says compiled and printed then, not the 2021 upload date
sources.contentReviewScope: Visually inspected cover, contents, illustrations list, introduction printed4–6, acknowledgements7, chapter opening29, and summary43–44 (PDF1–8,33–36,55–56, including intervening illustrations).

sources.title: Timeline of Potawatomi History
sources.author: Forest County Potawatomi Community; no individual byline displayed
sources.annotation: A substantial community chronology, counted as one work. Selected institutional entries add a Wisconsin perspective rather than a universal Anishinaabe history. Origin dates, treaty totals, population figures and imprecise legal labels are excluded. The timeline's endpoint is not evidence of present operations.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual full timeline body read, web lines59–171; synthesis uses 1937 and 1994–2002 institutional entries. A later same-day refetch timed out after successful initial inspection.

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Public history in a Potawatomi museum
claimBlocks.text: Citizen Potawatomi Nation's 2018 account of its Cultural Heritage Center presents oral tradition as a way of carrying history. Director Kelli Mosteller and artist Jennifer Randell explain how public interpretation connects ancestral experience with present responsibilities and future generations. Their account addresses colonial disruption while emphasizing continuity and renewal. This is a particular museum's interpretation, useful alongside other community voices; it should not become a universal prophetic timetable for every Anishinaabe nation.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Article opening, named interpreters' comments and closing statements; lines41–47,60–67

claimBlocks.text: The Pokagon Band's history places Potawatomi relationships with Ojibwe and Odawa within the Three Fires while acknowledging differing origin accounts. It then follows a particular community's efforts to remain in its Great Lakes homeland under removal pressure. The account treats Congress's 1994 reaffirmation of federal recognition as recognition of an already existing people. Pokagon continuity therefore adds a distinct perspective; it cannot stand for every Potawatomi community's experience or the governments of all Anishinaabe peoples.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: History, opening paragraph and Leopold Pokagon/recognition passages; lines511,516–522

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Odawa belonging and changing land use
claimBlocks.text: The Little Traverse Bay Bands' 2005 history explains that Anishinaabe expresses a relationship shared with Ojibwe and Potawatomi, while a person's band or tribe remains more specific. Drawing on documents and elder interviews, the book follows Waganakising Odawa land use through settlement pressure, reduced seasonal movement, land loss and growing wage employment. Its account also describes continuing practices through change. This is a locally grounded history of particular Odawa bands, rather than one history for all Anishinaabe communities.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Printed introduction4–6, acknowledgements7, chapter opening29, summary43–44; PDF4–6,8,33,55–56

claimBlocks.text: Forest County Potawatomi's historical timeline follows a particular Wisconsin community through political reorganization and institution building. Its later entries record a Tribal Court in 1994, a tribal newspaper in 1995, and a museum with a People of the Three Fires exhibit in 2002. These dated entries show different settings in which community life and public history developed. They describe Forest County institutions, not a single government shared by all Potawatomi or Anishinaabe peoples, and do not verify current operations.

integrationNotes: Keep existing p14-s2 identity/provenance when renewing an14-c1; this is not a fifth/new work.
Three Fires duty labels conflict across CPN, Pokagon and Forest County accounts. Omit a universal duty chart; do not silently resolve the disagreement.
One LTBB book and one Forest County timeline each count once; their separate pages, illustrations and entries are not extra works.
LTBB publication is November2005, not2021. Author research/writing credit is printed7; no author ancestry inferred.
No copied illustrations, ceremonial directions, family-record transcription, current population total or universal migration date. Public access does not establish image-reuse permission.
researchGaps: These four situated US community perspectives are not a comprehensive account of Anishinaabe identities, territories, governments or oral traditions.
No independent treaty-text or court-record audit in this bounded packet; legal narrative claims remain excluded.
LTBB middle chapters beyond selected pages were not read. Forest County later refetch timed out; initial complete-body inspection supplied the evidence.
